name: Lunar Prospector
first: Neutron-spectrometer hydrogen finding at both lunar poles
description: The third NASA Discovery-class mission and the first NASA-managed dedicated lunar orbiter of the post-Apollo era. Launched 1998-01-07 on an Athena II from Cape Canaveral, Lunar Prospector entered a 100-km circular polar lunar orbit on 1998-01-11. The 296-kg spinning spacecraft carried five instruments: a gamma-ray spectrometer for global crustal composition, a neutron spectrometer for hydrogen / water-ice detection at the poles, an alpha-particle spectrometer for radon gas (indirect volcanism detection), a magnetometer + electron reflectometer for crustal magnetism, and a Doppler gravity experiment. Boynton-team analysis of the neutron data (Feldman et al., Science 281 + 284) found sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles — consistent with ~2 × 10⁹ tonnes of hydrogen-rich material (probably water ice) in permanently shadowed polar craters. Mission ended 1999-07-31 with deliberate impact near Shackleton crater hoping to release a detectable water-vapour plume; none was seen. The hydrogen finding stood until LCROSS and Chandrayaan-1 / M3 (2009) provided independent confirmation.

events.label: LAUNCH
events.note: Athena II from Cape Canaveral SLC-46 1998-01-07 02:28 UTC.

events.label: LOI
events.note: Lunar orbit insertion 1998-01-11 — initial 100 × 100 km polar orbit.

events.label: POLAR HYDROGEN
events.note: Neutron-spectrometer detects sharp neutron-flux deficits over both lunar poles — strong hydrogen signal, consistent with polar water ice.

events.label: SHACKLETON IMPACT
events.note: Deliberate impact near Shackleton crater 1999-07-31 09:52 UTC. No water-vapour plume detected from Earth.
